newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU mulls action to fight international bribery.
newsitem.headline: EU mulls action to fight international bribery.

text.p: The European Commission is considering legislation to force national governments in the European Union to fight international bribery, an area where the EU lags far behind the United States.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said on Wednesday that the Commission could use Article 101 of the EC treaty barring national legislation or administrative practices that distort fair trade and competition.

The remarks, made at a conference on corruption in international business transactions, were a reference to the still widespread practice in the EU of tolerating bribes by companies to foreign officials to win international contracts.

"The possible use of (Article 101) is being considered by the Commission," Van Miert said. The conference was organised by Transparency International, a non-governmental body created in 1993 to fight corruption.
Van Miert also complained about the practice by some countries of allowing companies to deduct bribes from corporate tax, without naming any countries.

Bribery to win contracts in other countries, either in or outside of the EU, especially large infrastucture and supply tenders, is still common practice despite recent efforts to combat this and other corruption in the EU. But it is difficult to measure economically because of its hidden nature.
A recent Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) meeting on the issue said that the most extensive analysis had been done by the United States.

The U.S. government found that over the past two years some 100 business deals worth $45 billion had allegedly been lost by U.S. companies because of bribery, the OECD's secretary-general Donald Johnston told the meeting.
Although governments condemn corruption involving their own officials, at least in principle, they often turn a blind eye when the same practices are used in the hunt for foreign contracts.
In Belgium, for example, international corruption is not only tolerated, but effectively encouraged by the tax deductibility of bribes.

"Although reprehensible, secret commissions are unfortunately necessary in trade or industrial relations with other countries," Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt said in July in reply to a written question by a Belgian senator.
This contrasts with strict legislation in the United States where the threat of prosecution is a strong deterrent.
"I think the (Foreign Corrupt Practices Act) has been rather effective in the United States," Van Miert said.
Article 101 allows the Commission to initiate legislation to promote free competition, but EU ministers would make the final decision by a qualified majority vote.
Van Miert said the article could also be used if needed to persuade EU states to implement a recent protocol aimed at fighting bribery of EU officials to obtain contracts or funds.
